record.paper_title: Reusing Space: Techniques and Open Problems
record.context_brief: beyond logarithmic circuit depth in CL
record.original_question: Can catalytic logspace compute every NC2 circuit, or at least every circuit of depth ω(log n)?

evidence.quote: Problem 14. Show that NC2, or even any circuit of ω(log n) depth, can be computed in CL.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Define catalytic logspace, denoted CL, as the class of languages decided by deterministic Turing machines equipped with: (i) a read-only input tape, (ii) a work tape of size O(log n), and (iii) an auxiliary "catalytic" tape of size polynomial in n that may be initialized with an arbitrary string and may be modified during the computation, provided that at the end of the computation its contents are restored to the original initialization (the machine must operate correctly for every initialization of the catalytic tape). Define NC^2 as the class of languages decided by uniform families of Boolean circuits over fan-in 2 AND/OR/NOT gates having polynomial size and O(log^2 n) depth.

Question: Show that NC^2 ⊆ CL. More generally, show that every language decided by a uniform family of polynomial-size Boolean circuits of depth ω(log n) is contained in CL.
artifact.status_search_result: The problem remains open. The best containment known is TC^1 ⊆ CL (Buhrman et al. 2014). Recent work (Alekseev et al., MFCS 2025 / arXiv:2504.17412) improves the space bound for SAC^2 to CSPACE(O(log^2 n / log log n), 2^{O(log^{1+ε} n)}), described as a step toward NC^2 ⊆ CL but not a resolution. No known result places all ω(log n)-depth circuits in CL.

status_evidence.title: Catalytic Computing and Register Programs Beyond Log-Depth
status_evidence.snippet: A further step towards showing NC^2 ⊆ CL; proves SAC^2 ⊆ CSPACE(O(log^2 n / log log n), 2^{O(log^{1+ε} n)}).
status_evidence.claim: NC^2 ⊆ CL remains open; recent partial progress on circuits beyond log-depth.

status_evidence.title: Catalytic Logspace: Complexity & Applications
status_evidence.snippet: Understanding CL remains a major open problem, as TC1 remains the most powerful containment to date.
status_evidence.claim: The best known containment in CL is TC^1; placing NC^2 in CL is still open.
